nameStory: Meadow pea gets its name from its favorite hangout spot - open meadows and grassy areas where it scrambles among other plants. The 'pea' part comes from its classic pea-family flowers and its membership in the legume family, making it a wild cousin of garden peas. You might also hear it called 'yellow pea' for its sunny-colored blooms or 'meadow vetchling' since it belongs to the vetch group of climbing legumes.
description: Meadow pea is a climbing perennial wildflower that can stretch up to 4 feet tall as it scrambles through grasses and other plants for support. This cheerful member of the pea family produces bright yellow flowers that look just like tiny sweet pea blossoms. It's a hardy plant that comes back year after year, slowly spreading through damp meadows and grasslands. Like other legumes, it helps enrich the soil by fixing nitrogen through special bacteria in its roots.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow pea-shaped flowers about half an inch long, with the classic 'butterfly' form of legumes - one large upper petal (banner), two side petals (wings), and a boat-shaped lower petal (keel). Flowers cluster in groups of 2-12 on long stalks.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with just one pair of narrow, grass-like leaflets that feel smooth and slightly waxy. Each leaf ends in branching tendrils that feel thin and wiry, helping the plant climb through surrounding vegetation.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A climbing or scrambling vine that uses its curly tendrils to grab onto grasses and other plants for support. Stems are angular rather than round and feel slightly ridged when you run your finger along them.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened brown pods about an inch long that split open with a slight 'pop' when ripe, revealing several round, hard seeds inside. Pods turn from green to brown as they mature.

habitat: Look for meadow pea in damp meadows, wet grasslands, and along stream edges where the soil stays moist. It thrives in open areas with plenty of grasses and other plants to climb through, often found in old fields, roadside ditches, and the edges of marshes. This plant prefers fertile, slightly alkaline soils and needs good moisture throughout the growing season.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground roots, sending up fresh green stems with their distinctive paired leaflets and curly tendrils. Plants begin their climbing growth as they search for support among emerging grasses.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow pea flowers bloom from June through August, attracting bees and other pollinators. This is the best time for identification when the distinctive yellow blooms are most visible above the surrounding vegetation.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and turn brown, eventually splitting open to scatter seeds. Leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only the perennial root system underground. Look for dried brown stems and empty seed pods as evidence of last year's growth.

funFact: Meadow pea is a special host plant for the delicate wood white butterfly, which lays its eggs exclusively on plants in the pea family - making this humble meadow climber a crucial nursery for one of Europe's most ethereal butterflies with wings so translucent they seem like flying tissue paper.
confusionNotes: The yellow flowers make meadow pea pretty distinctive among New England's wild peas, but you might confuse the climbing habit with other vetchlings. Remember: yellow flowers = meadow pea, while most other wild peas in our region have purple, pink, or white blooms.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'pea,' this wild plant isn't closely related to garden peas and shouldn't be eaten. Like many legumes, it was historically used as livestock fodder, which explains why it sometimes shows up in old farm fields where it was once cultivated.
compareHints: Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms. The narrow, grass-like leaflets in pairs also distinguish it from broad-leaved sweet pea, which has much wider leaflets. If you see yellow pea-family flowers climbing through a meadow, you've likely found meadow pea.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color.
